source.title: The Effect of Network Width on Stochastic Gradient Descent and Generalization: an Empirical Study
source.authors: Daniel S. Park; Jascha Narain Sohl-Dickstein; Quoc V. Le; Samuel L. Smith

record.file_problem: Full text supplied, including supplementary material.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports training and test results across network widths, parameterizations, and batch-normalization settings, but its outcomes concern test accuracy, optimal SGD noise scale, and numerical stability rather than training classification error or the claim versions’ specified outcomes.
record.gate_note: It reports test accuracy and failure rates, not training classification error. The training-time threshold based on test accuracy is a run-selection rule, not a training-error result. The cited results from other studies are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study uses critical ReLU initialization, citing He et al. and Schoenholz et al., but does not test its effect on learning speed or trainable depth. Its own results concern late-time test accuracy, optimal SGD noise scale, and numerical stability. These do not establish any version's specified effect. In particular, numerical failures are not measured relative to an initial linearized stability threshold, and batch-normalization experiments do not establish faster training or greater learning-rate tolerance in matched comparisons.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is substantially correct. Without batch normalization, the normalized noise scale maximizing test accuracy is proportional to width, and wider networks achieve better best observed test accuracy. With batch normalization, the analogous optimal-hyperparameter trend persists for residual networks but differs for CNNs; this exception does not mean CNN test accuracy fails to improve with width. The authors also conclude that bounded stable learning rates force the largest batch size compatible with optimal noise to decrease with width.
record.recipe_differences: The experiments study width-dependent SGD hyperparameters and test accuracy, not the claim’s training-error outcomes.
record.method_sensitivity: The test-accuracy and optimal-noise-scale trends vary with parameterization, batch normalization, network family, width, learning rate, and batch size; CIFAR-10 WRNs in the standard scheme require a smaller learning rate at wider settings for numerical stability.

fits_no_version.finding: Without batch normalization, the normalized noise scale maximizing late-time test accuracy grows approximately proportionally to width across the tested families and parameterizations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The optimal normalized SGD noise scale for generalization increases with network width in the tested settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Best observed test accuracy increases with width. With batch normalization, WRNs retain the width-dependent optimal-hyperparameter trend, whereas CNNs show a weaker or different relationship.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Width improves best observed generalization, with architecture-dependent relationships between width and optimal hyperparameters under batch normalization.

fits_no_version.finding: Section H measures numerical-error failure rates over 20 runs per setting after 20 epochs at batch size 64. Stability curves approximately align across widths under normalized learning rates, with a subtler relationship for MLPs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Numerical stability depends on learning rate, width, and parameterization; normalized learning rates approximately align stability boundaries in the tested families.

fits_no_version.finding: Section I finds architecture-dependent differences in peak test accuracy between standard and NTK parameterizations, while keeping the critical initialization scale fixed.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The generalization advantage of standard versus NTK parameterization depends on network architecture.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 97, 2019
record.problems: The evidence relevant to the broader claim is indirect: the reported performance metric is test accuracy rather than training error. The authors note that the experiments may not probe asymptotic behavior and that larger-width experiments were not performed. Several findings are presented as plots, and the text does not provide their individual numerical values.
record.rows_left_out: No rows: reported outcomes measure test accuracy, optimal normalized noise scale, or numerical failure rate, none of which is a specified training-error result in V1–V6.

untested.parts: Training classification error, including near-zero error on ordinary or corrupted labels; effects of size, early stopping, and regularization on that error.
Spurious local minima in realizable two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems and their reduction through student overparameterization.
Training-error degradation with depth, its prevention by identity shortcuts, and the stated initialization alternatives.
Effects of activation-matched initialization on signal propagation, learning speed, and trainable depth; orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization.
Loss and curvature dynamics relative to the initial linearized stability limit; catapult recovery, edge-of-stability training, and divergence from below the threshold.
Matched comparisons establishing faster training or higher learning-rate tolerance with batch normalization, and equivalent training using Fixup.

record.verdict_notes: Keeping the result rows empty is appropriate. The test-accuracy cutoff is a run-selection rule, not evidence of training classification error. Existing rows_left_out already declares the omitted test-accuracy, noise-scale, and numerical-failure outcomes.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error, corrupted or random labels, CIFAR-100, and the stated effects of model size, early stopping, and regularization on training error.
Teacher-student ReLU problems, spurious local minima, and student width relative to teacher width.
Depth effects on training error, identity shortcuts, very deep plain tanh networks, and residual networks without normalization.
Comparisons of activation-matched initializations, signal or gradient propagation, training speed, trainable depth, orthogonal versus Gaussian weights, and 10,000-layer plain convolutional networks.
Loss behavior and curvature around or above stability limits, sharpness over training, and divergence relative to those limits.
Training-speed and learning-rate-tolerance comparisons for batch normalization, and Fixup training without normalization.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
